paragraphs.heading: Continents on the move
paragraphs.text: Continental drift means that Earth's continents move relative to one another over geologic time. In the early 20th century, when it was first proposed as a scientific theory, the notion that continents could move was widely rejected. Since then it has been extensively validated. It is now part of the science of plate tectonics, which studies how the continents move as they ride on plates of Earth's lithosphere.

paragraphs.heading: An early guess from a map
paragraphs.text: The speculation that continents might have drifted was first raised by Abraham Ortelius in 1596. He suggested that earthquakes and floods had "torn away" the Americas from Europe and Africa. The traces of that rupture, he wrote, show themselves to anyone who lays out a world map and looks carefully at the coasts of the three continents.

paragraphs.heading: The case for fixed continents
paragraphs.text: In his Manual of Geology of 1863, Dana wrote that the general outline of the continents and oceans was set in earliest time. Dana was enormously influential in America, and this idea became known as the Permanence theory. The Challenger expedition of 1872–1876 seemed to confirm it. Its exploration of the deep sea beds showed that land debris carried to the ocean by rivers settles comparatively near the shore, on what is now called the continental shelf. That suggested the oceans were a permanent feature of Earth's surface.

paragraphs.heading: Wegener's Pangaea
paragraphs.text: On 6 January 1912 Alfred Wegener laid out his hypothesis before the German Geological Society for the first time. He proposed that the continents had once made up a single landmass, which he named Pangaea, and that it broke apart and the pieces drifted to where they are now. He expanded the concept into a book published in 1915, The Origin of Continents and Oceans. The phrase "continental drift" was first used by Wegener.

paragraphs.heading: Not the only one
paragraphs.text: Several scientists before Wegener's 1912 paper had put forward the idea that the American continents once formed a single landmass with Eurasia and Africa. Roberto Mantovani conjectured, in 1889 and again in 1909, that every continent had once been joined into one supercontinent. Frank Bursley Taylor suggested in 1908 that the continents were moved to their present positions by a process he called "continental creep". Taylor was the first to realize that moving continents would build mountains, and he put the Himalayas down to the collision of the Indian subcontinent with Asia. Wegener said that of all those theories, Taylor's was the most like his own.

paragraphs.heading: Why it was rejected
paragraphs.text: Wegener presented much evidence for drift, but he could not give a convincing explanation of the physical processes that might have caused it. He suggested two things that might have pulled the continents apart: the centrifugal pseudoforce of the spinning Earth, or a small part of astronomical precession. Calculations showed that the force was not enough. He also put the speed of continental motion at 250 cm/year, which was implausibly high. By the rate accepted today, the Americas are separating from Europe and Africa at about 2.5 cm/year. He was taken less seriously as well because he was not a geologist.

paragraphs.heading: A proposed mechanism
paragraphs.text: Arthur Holmes, an English geologist, championed continental drift when the theory was deeply unfashionable. In 1931 he proposed that Earth's mantle contained convection cells. These cells, he said, shed the heat that radioactive decay produces and moved the crust at the surface. Wegener did not live to see his hypothesis triumph, but continental drift is now generally accepted. Even today, the details of the forces that propel the plates are poorly understood.
